title.en: Sliding-Window KV Cache: Capping Memory for Long Conversations

description.en: A KV cache that keeps every token forever eventually runs out of GPU memory. Production long-context models cap it instead — learn the sliding-window eviction trick that keeps memory flat no matter how long the chat runs.

story_variants.en:
## The Cache That Never Stops Growing

"You measured the KV cache's price tag," Vaathiyaar says, "now imagine a conversation that runs for an hour. Or a day. If the cache keeps every token's key and value forever, memory grows without bound — eventually there's no GPU big enough."

### The Fix: Only Remember Recently

Many production systems don't try to remember the *entire* conversation. Instead they use a **sliding-window cache**: keep only the most recent `window` tokens' K/V pairs, and **evict** — permanently drop — anything older. Mistral's sliding-window attention and StreamingLLM-style setups both lean on this idea.

```
cache:  [tok1, tok2, tok3, tok4, tok5, tok6]
window = 3
evict -> keep only the last 3 -> [tok4, tok5, tok6]
```

Once the window is full, adding a new token means dropping the oldest one — memory stays flat forever, no matter how long the conversation runs. The tradeoff is real: the model literally can't attend to anything older than `window` tokens, so very-long-range facts can fall out of the cache entirely. That's a deliberate choice, not a bug — it trades a little long-range recall for a hard memory ceiling.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** unbounded cache growth is a production outage waiting to happen. A sliding window turns 'memory grows forever' into 'memory is a constant you chose.'

Today you implement the eviction step itself — the one line of logic that keeps a long-running chat's memory bounded.
